screens.title: Directory-Based Coherence
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how directory-based coherence replaces system-wide broadcast with targeted, point-to-point messages. The directory is a per-block record — often distributed across memory controllers — that records the block state, which cores share it, and which core owns a writable copy. This structure avoids the broadcast storms that make snooping impractical at large scale, but it trades off storage and directory access overhead. We'll look at how read and write requests are handled, how sharer lists are represented, and the practical techniques — coarse bit vectors, limited pointers, and hierarchical directories — used to reduce storage. You'll also compare latency and bandwidth differences with snooping, and walk through a hands-on sequence that shows exactly how directory entries and messages evolve during reads and writes. By the end, you should be able to explain why a directory is necessary beyond a certain system size, how directory storage grows with core count and memory size, and what system-level trade-offs influence whether to distribute the directory or centralize it. Consider: at what system size does broadcast become more expensive than directory bookkeeping?

keyIdea.text: Directories record who holds each memory block and let the system send messages only to relevant caches, enabling scalable coherence without global broadcasts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Directory-Based Coherence
Directory-Based Coherence
Point-to-point coherence for large multiprocessors

Directory entries track a block's state, which caches share it, and who owns a writable copy. This lets systems send messages only to relevant caches, avoiding broadcast traffic at scale.

In this lesson
Read/write handling, sharer-list strategies, latency vs bandwidth trade-offs, and distributed directory techniques.
Why it matters
For systems beyond a few dozen cores, broadcast-based snooping overwhelms interconnects; directories let coherence scale to hundreds or thousands of cores when designed carefully.
Explore key topics
Directory Entry
State, sharer bit vector, owner pointer — the per-block phone book.
Sharer Compression
Coarse vectors, limited pointers, and hierarchical designs trade accuracy for storage.
Directory vs Snooping
Point-to-point reduces bandwidth at scale; snooping gives lower latency for small sockets.
Concept map
Directory
Per-block entry tracking state, sharers, owner.
Point-to-point
Messages sent only to relevant caches.
Sharer lists
Bit vectors or compressed representations.
Scalability
Distributed directories reduce bottlenecks.
Coming up: read/write flows and storage trade-offs.

screens.title: Directory: structure and per-block entry
screens.narratorSegment: A directory entry is the unit of truth for a memory block. Concretely, it stores three fields: the block state, the sharer list, and the owner pointer. The state captures whether the block is Uncached, Shared, or Modified. The sharer list tells which caches hold read-only copies, typically as an N-bit vector for N cores. The owner pointer identifies the cache that currently holds a writable copy when the state is Modified. Why these fields? The state tells the directory how to service requests; the sharer list lets it send messages only to caches that might hold stale copies; and the owner pointer lets the directory forward requests to the single writer to retrieve the latest data. A common misconception is thinking the directory holds data — it does not. It holds metadata and pointers. For example, when a block is Modified at P3, owner points to P3, the state is Modified, and the sharer list is empty. If another core reads, the directory forwards the read to P3 so it can supply the clean data and transition both cores to Shared. The core insight is that this small per-block record replaces system-wide broadcasts with targeted messages, at the cost of storing these fields for each block. How does that storage scale in your designs?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Directory entries keep state, a sharer list, and an owner pointer so the system can route coherence messages without global broadcasts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Directory Entry
Per-block entry
State • Sharers • Owner
State: Uncached, Shared, or Modified. Guides how requests are routed.
Sharers: Bit vector indicating caches that hold the block in Shared state.
Owner: Cache ID of the writer when state is Modified; otherwise memory controller.
Analogy
Think of the directory as a phone book listing who has a copy and who is the current writer.
Key Takeaway

The directory stores metadata for routing coherence messages; it must be present per memory block to avoid broadcast-based snooping.

Example state snapshot
Block 0
State: Modified
Sharers: 0000... (none)
Owner: P3
Block 1
State: Shared
Sharers: P1, P2
Owner: memory controller
Common misconception: the directory does not contain the block's payload. It contains only metadata and pointers used to route data and invalidation messages to the caches that actually hold the data.

screens.title: Read request handling
screens.narratorSegment: When a cache issues a read, it sends a read request to the directory. The directory consults the entry and follows one of three paths. If the block is Uncached, the directory forwards the request to memory, retrieves data, changes state to Shared, and adds the requester to the sharer list. If the block is already Shared, the directory may forward the request to an existing sharer or to memory, and then include the new requester in the sharer list. If the block is Modified, the directory forwards the request to the owner cache. The owner sends the most recent data and typically downgrades its copy to Shared, and the directory updates the sharer list to include both owner and requester. A concrete example: P1 reads block 0; directory sees Uncached, fetches from memory, marks Shared and adds P1. Later P2 reads the same block; directory sees Shared and adds P2 to the sharer vector. A common misconception is that reads always go to memory; with a directory they often go to caches that already have the data, reducing memory traffic. Key takeaway: directory lookups let the system route reads efficiently, but each request pays the directory lookup cost and any forwarding cost to owners or sharers.

keyIdea.title: Read Flow
keyIdea.text: Directory routes read requests to memory or existing sharers/owner, then updates the sharer list to reflect new readers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Read Request Handling
Read request flow
Uncached • Shared • Modified paths
Uncached: Directory asks memory, sets state to Shared, adds requester to sharers.
Shared: Directory forwards to a sharer or memory, then appends requester to sharer list.
Modified: Directory forwards to owner; owner supplies data and downgrades to Shared; directory updates sharers.
Example
P1 reads block 0 (Uncached) → memory replies → directory adds P1 as sharer. P2 later reads → directory adds P2; now both are sharers.
Diagrammatic steps
1. Cache sends read request to directory.
2. Directory checks state and forwards request appropriately.
3. Directory updates sharer list and state as needed.
4. Data is returned to requester from memory or owner/sharer.
Misconception check: the directory is not a cache of data. It only points you to where the data currently resides so read requests can be satisfied without unnecessary broadcasts.

screens.title: Write request handling
screens.narratorSegment: A write request asks to obtain a writable copy. The directory again checks the state and acts differently depending on it. If Uncached, the directory grants Modified to the requester and sets the owner pointer accordingly after fetching or granting exclusivity. If Shared, the directory must revoke read-only copies: it sends invalidation messages to all sharers and waits for acknowledgements. Only after all sharers have invalidated do we transition to Modified and set the requester as owner. If Modified, the directory forwards the request to the current owner so the owner can supply data or perform a writeback; the directory then updates the owner to the new requester. A practical example: if P1 and P2 share a block and P3 wants to write, the directory issues invalidations to P1 and P2; when acknowledgements arrive the directory marks the block Modified with owner P3. A common misconception is that invalidations are instantaneous; they require messages and acknowledgements, and those round trips contribute to latency. Key idea: writes require coordination to ensure no stale read-only copies remain, and the directory orchestrates this point-to-point sequence to avoid broadcasts in large systems.

keyIdea.title: Write Flow
keyIdea.text: Writes require invalidating sharers or transferring ownership; the directory coordinates this to guarantee exclusive writable copies.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Write Request Handling
Write request flow
Invalidations, owner transfer, and writeback handling
Uncached: Directory grants Modified and sets owner to requester.
Shared: Directory sends invalidations to all sharers, waits for ACKs, then grants Modified to requester.
Modified: Directory forwards request to owner; owner supplies data and invalidates its copy; ownership transfers to requester.
Scenario
P1 and P2 share block 0. P3 writes: directory issues invalidations to P1 and P2, waits for acknowledgements, then sets owner=P3 and state=Modified.
Message types
  • Read request/response
  • Invalidation and invalidation ACK
  • Forward-to-owner and writeback
Misconception check: ownership transfer often includes a writeback or data-forward so the directory can maintain memory consistency; ownership is carried via messages, not by simple pointer updates alone.

screens.title: Directory vs. Snooping
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing directory and snooping protocols highlights when each is appropriate. Snooping uses broadcast over a shared bus or interconnect: every cache observes coherence messages, which yields low latency on small systems because no directory lookup is required. However, snooping does not scale: broadcasts consume bandwidth and increase contention as the number of cores grows. Directory protocols use point-to-point messages, which scale well and keep bandwidth lower at large core counts, but they require per-block directory storage and an extra lookup latency at the directory controller. Storage is a major downside: an N-core system using a full bit vector needs N bits per block, which quickly becomes impractical. Bandwidth behavior flips with scale: snooping has lower per-request latency small-scale but higher total bandwidth cost at scale; directory has the opposite profile. A useful mental model: snooping is a town square where every announcement is heard by all; directories are the post office delivering messages only to the addresses that matter. The key question to ask when designing a system is the expected core count and where broadcasts become more costly than directory bookkeeping and the directory's additional access latency.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Snooping favors low-latency small systems; directories favor scalable, bandwidth-efficient large systems at the expense of storage and lookup latency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Directory vs Snooping
Snooping
Broadcast-based coherence
  • Low latency for small numbers of cores
  • High broadcast bandwidth as cores increase
  • Little directory storage required
Directory
Point-to-point, per-block metadata
  • Scales to many cores with lower bandwidth cost
  • Higher per-request latency due to directory lookup
  • Significant storage overhead per memory block
Design rule of thumb
Snooping works well for 2–16 cores; directories become attractive beyond that range because broadcast costs dominate link bandwidth and contention.

screens.title: Sharer lists and storage growth
screens.narratorSegment: Sharer lists are the most direct way to know which cores hold a block: one bit per core. Unfortunately, this simple approach scales poorly. For N cores and M blocks, storing N bits per block yields M × N bits total. The chapter gives an example: with 1024 cores, each sharer list is 1024 bits (128 bytes), and multiplying by a large number of blocks quickly becomes impractical. That drives several compression strategies. Coarse bit vectors group cores so one bit represents multiple cores — this reduces storage but sometimes requires broadcasting within a group. Limited pointers store only a few sharer IDs; if the number of sharers exceeds the limit, the directory falls back to broadcasting or a different mechanism. Hierarchical directories break the system into levels so a top-level directory points to lower-level directories that manage subsets of cores. Each approach trades storage for additional messaging, potential broadcasts to groups, or added complexity. A misconception is assuming compression is free; compressed representations increase protocol complexity and can add latency or additional messages. When designing, always weigh the storage saved against the extra messaging cost and complexity introduced by the chosen compression technique.

keyIdea.title: Sharer List Scaling
keyIdea.text: N-bit sharer lists are simple but large; coarse vectors, limited pointers, and hierarchical directories trade storage for messaging and complexity.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Sharer Lists & Storage
Problem: N-bit growth
Storage grows as N × M where N is cores and M is blocks.
Example: 1024 cores → 1024-bit sharer list per block (128 bytes). If memory has many blocks, directory storage becomes impractical.
Compression techniques
  • Coarse bit vectors: one bit per group of cores; reduces bits but may require group broadcast.
  • Limited pointers: store a small number of sharer IDs; fallback to broadcast if exceeded.
  • Hierarchical directories: multiple levels manage subsets to reduce per-entry size.
Design trade-off
Compression reduces storage but can add messaging or require fallbacks. Always analyze how often fallbacks will occur for your workload before committing to a compression strategy.

screens.title: Directory bandwidth and distribution
screens.narratorSegment: The directory controller must process every coherence request for the addresses it owns. In a centralized design, that controller can become a bandwidth and latency bottleneck as core counts increase. Directory bandwidth describes how many requests per second the directory controller can handle; when requests queue up, directory access latency increases. Two widely used solutions are distribution and caching. Distributed directories place directory responsibility across multiple memory controllers or cache banks, each covering a subset of addresses. This spreads load and reduces the chance of a single hotspot. Directory caching keeps frequently accessed directory entries close to requestors so lookups avoid the full directory controller on every request. Distributed directories reduce traffic concentration but complicate address mapping and failure modes. Directory caching reduces repeated lookup costs but introduces coherence for directory entries themselves. A common misconception is that distribution removes all bottlenecks — it reduces them but introduces design complexity such as remapping and cross-controller coordination. The practical lesson is to balance distribution granularity and directory caching based on expected access locality and workload hotspots. Directory bandwidth and distribution means distribute directory entries and cache hot entries to avoid single-controller bottlenecks; both approaches add design complexity and trade-offs.. In practical terms, why directories become bottlenecks and how distribution helps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Distribute directory entries and cache hot entries to avoid single-controller bottlenecks; both approaches add design complexity and trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Bandwidth & Distribution
Directory bandwidth
Controller must handle all coherence messages for its addresses.
Queueing at the directory increases access time. For large systems, a single controller can limit throughput and raise tail latencies.
Mitigations
  • Distributed directories: scatter directory entries to multiple memory controllers to spread load.
  • Directory caching: keep hot directory entries cached near requesters to avoid repeated lookups.
Design note: distribution reduces hotspot probability but complicates address-to-directory mapping and cross-controller coordination.

screens.title: Directory access time and latency impact
screens.narratorSegment: Every directory-based coherence operation pays the cost of a directory lookup. For modest core counts, that extra lookup can make directory protocols slower than snooping. The chapter notes directory access time can be on the order of 10 to 20 cycles in systems with over 100 cores, which is acceptable for large systems but noticeable for latency-sensitive workloads. The end-to-end latency of a coherence request includes the cache request, directory lookup, any forwarding to owners or sharers, and the data return. Because directories often avoid broadcasts, they usually reduce total network bandwidth but add serialized steps: lookup, forwarding, and acknowledgements. Designers can mitigate this by distributing directories to reduce lookup contention and by caching directory entries to avoid repeated full lookups. A misconception is thinking directory latency is fixed; it depends on directory placement, caching, and request contention. When designing for latency-sensitive applications, measure the full request path and consider whether snooping inside a socket plus directory across sockets gives a better latency-bandwidth balance. Directory access time and latency impact means directory lookups add latency to each request; distribution and caching reduce lookup time but add complexity.. In practical terms, how directory lookups affect request latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Access Time & Latency
Latency components
Directory lookup is one of several serialized steps.
  • Cache request to directory
  • Directory lookup time
  • Forwarding to owner/sharers and their responses
  • Data return to requester
When it matters

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Hands-on Simulation
Storage calculation
Fields: state=2 bits, sharer list=16 bits, owner=4 bits → 22 bits per entry
// Per-entry bits: 2 + 16 + 4 = 22 bits
entries = 256
total_bits = 22 * entries      // 5632 bits
total_bytes = total_bits / 8   // 704 bytes
This small example fits in under 1 KB, but scaling N or blocks M quickly increases storage demands.
Simulation sequence
Sequence: P1: Read 0; P2: Read 0; P3: Write 0; P1: Read 0
1) P1: Read 0
 - Dir sees Uncached -> Dir->Memory request
 - Memory replies -> Dir sets state=Shared, sharers={P1}
 - Messages: P1->Dir (read req), Dir->Memory, Memory->Dir (data), Dir->P1 (data)

2) P2: Read 0
 - Dir sees Shared -> Dir adds P2 to sharers
 - Messages: P2->Dir (read req), Dir->P2 (data)

3) P3: Write 0
 - Dir sees Shared -> Dir sends Invalidates to P1 and P2
 - P1,P2 send ACKs -> Dir sets state=Modified, owner=P3
 - Messages: P3->Dir(write req), Dir->P1(invalidate), Dir->P2(invalidate), P1->Dir(ACK), P2->Dir(ACK), Dir->P3(grant)

4) P1: Read 0
 - Dir sees Modified(owner=P3) -> Dir forwards read to P3
 - P3 supplies data and downgrades to Shared -> Dir updates sharers={P3,P1}
 - Messages: P1->Dir(read req), Dir->P3(forward), P3->Dir(data & state update), Dir->P1(data)
Key takeaway

The directory avoids broadcasts by targeting messages, but each request incurs directory lookups and targeted messaging costs; compare message counts and latency with snooping for your workload.

screens.title: Message count comparison: directory vs snooping
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare message counts for the simulated sequence to highlight trade-offs. In the directory approach each operation involves directory messages plus targeted forwards: reads required directory requests and data returns; the write required two invalidations and their acknowledgements in addition to the write request and grant. Snooping, by contrast, would broadcast coherence requests: P1's first read would still fetch from memory, but the write by P3 would broadcast an invalidation to all caches on the bus. Message counts for snooping can be lower per-request if many caches observe the broadcast naturally, but total network bandwidth grows with the number of listeners and frequent broadcasts. In our four-step example, directory messaging is targeted: invalidations go only to P1 and P2; snooping would hit every cache. The directory reduces system-wide noise, at the cost of directory lookups and per-request coordination. The lesson: count messages and consider the interconnect cost per broadcast when choosing between protocols. Also consider latency-sensitive paths: snooping avoids directory lookup steps but pays with broader network traffic and contention. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how directory-based coherence replaces system-wide broadcast with targeted, point-to-point messages. The directory is a per-block record — often distributed across memory controllers — that records the block state, which cores share it, and which core owns a writable copy. This structure avoids the broadcast storms that make snooping impractical at large scale, but it trades off storage and directory access overhead. We'll look at how read and write requests are handled, how sharer lists are represented, and the practical techniques — coarse bit vectors, limited pointers, and hierarchical directories — used to reduce storage. You'll also compare latency and bandwidth differences with snooping, and walk through a hands-on sequence that shows exactly how directory entries and messages evolve during reads and writes. By the end, you should be able to explain why a directory is necessary beyond a certain system size, how directory storage grows with core count and memory size, and what system-level trade-offs influence whether to distribute the directory or centralize it. Consider: at what system size does broadcast become more expensive than directory bookkeeping?

These objectives guide the chapter. First, you'll be able to describe how a directory-based coherence protocol stores and updates per-block information. That means explaining the three core fields: the block state, the sharer list, and the owner pointer, and why each is necessary. Second, you'll compare directory protocols with snooping, focusing on scalability, latency, and bandwidth. You'll learn when snooping's low latency is preferable and when directory point-to-point messaging becomes essential. Third, you'll read and follow directory entry formats and analyze how the sharer list scales with N cores, including concrete compression techniques like coarse bit vectors and limited pointers. Finally, you'll analyze design trade-offs between centralized, distributed, and hierarchical directories, and how directory caching or distribution reduces bottlenecks. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have mastered it. Think about which objective feels most unfamiliar now and we'll build toward it step by step.

Continuing the objectives, you'll practice tracing read and write flows through a directory, including the messages a directory sends and the state transitions it records. You'll also calculate directory storage for a small system and evaluate techniques that reduce storage cost. Practically, that means performing a small design exercise: compute the total storage for a directory with fixed bits per field and simulate a sequence of reads and writes to observe messages and directory updates. Finally, you'll be able to articulate the reasons for hybrid protocols that use snooping inside a socket and directories between sockets, and explain the trade-offs that lead to that hybrid choice. Each objective includes a competency check: after the simulation you should list the messages generated and explain why a directory used compression or fallback broadcasts. If you can do that, you've met the practical objectives.

A directory entry is the unit of truth for a memory block. Concretely, it stores three fields: the block state, the sharer list, and the owner pointer. The state captures whether the block is Uncached, Shared, or Modified. The sharer list tells which caches hold read-only copies, typically as an N-bit vector for N cores. The owner pointer identifies the cache that currently holds a writable copy when the state is Modified. Why these fields? The state tells the directory how to service requests; the sharer list lets it send messages only to caches that might hold stale copies; and the owner pointer lets the directory forward requests to the single writer to retrieve the latest data. A common misconception is thinking the directory holds data — it does not. It holds metadata and pointers. For example, when a block is Modified at P3, owner points to P3, the state is Modified, and the sharer list is empty. If another core reads, the directory forwards the read to P3 so it can supply the clean data and transition both cores to Shared. The core insight is that this small per-block record replaces system-wide broadcasts with targeted messages, at the cost of storing these fields for each block. How does that storage scale in your designs?

When a cache issues a read, it sends a read request to the directory. The directory consults the entry and follows one of three paths. If the block is Uncached, the directory forwards the request to memory, retrieves data, changes state to Shared, and adds the requester to the sharer list. If the block is already Shared, the directory may forward the request to an existing sharer or to memory, and then include the new requester in the sharer list. If the block is Modified, the directory forwards the request to the owner cache. The owner sends the most recent data and typically downgrades its copy to Shared, and the directory updates the sharer list to include both owner and requester. A concrete example: P1 reads block 0; directory sees Uncached, fetches from memory, marks Shared and adds P1. Later P2 reads the same block; directory sees Shared and adds P2 to the sharer vector. A common misconception is that reads always go to memory; with a directory they often go to caches that already have the data, reducing memory traffic. Key takeaway: directory lookups let the system route reads efficiently, but each request pays the directory lookup cost and any forwarding cost to owners or sharers.

A write request asks to obtain a writable copy. The directory again checks the state and acts differently depending on it. If Uncached, the directory grants Modified to the requester and sets the owner pointer accordingly after fetching or granting exclusivity. If Shared, the directory must revoke read-only copies: it sends invalidation messages to all sharers and waits for acknowledgements. Only after all sharers have invalidated do we transition to Modified and set the requester as owner. If Modified, the directory forwards the request to the current owner so the owner can supply data or perform a writeback; the directory then updates the owner to the new requester. A practical example: if P1 and P2 share a block and P3 wants to write, the directory issues invalidations to P1 and P2; when acknowledgements arrive the directory marks the block Modified with owner P3. A common misconception is that invalidations are instantaneous; they require messages and acknowledgements, and those round trips contribute to latency. Key idea: writes require coordination to ensure no stale read-only copies remain, and the directory orchestrates this point-to-point sequence to avoid broadcasts in large systems.

Comparing directory and snooping protocols highlights when each is appropriate. Snooping uses broadcast over a shared bus or interconnect: every cache observes coherence messages, which yields low latency on small systems because no directory lookup is required. However, snooping does not scale: broadcasts consume bandwidth and increase contention as the number of cores grows. Directory protocols use point-to-point messages, which scale well and keep bandwidth lower at large core counts, but they require per-block directory storage and an extra lookup latency at the directory controller. Storage is a major downside: an N-core system using a full bit vector needs N bits per block, which quickly becomes impractical. Bandwidth behavior flips with scale: snooping has lower per-request latency small-scale but higher total bandwidth cost at scale; directory has the opposite profile. A useful mental model: snooping is a town square where every announcement is heard by all; directories are the post office delivering messages only to the addresses that matter. The key question to ask when designing a system is the expected core count and where broadcasts become more costly than directory bookkeeping and the directory's additional access latency.

Sharer lists are the most direct way to know which cores hold a block: one bit per core. Unfortunately, this simple approach scales poorly. For N cores and M blocks, storing N bits per block yields M × N bits total. The chapter gives an example: with 1024 cores, each sharer list is 1024 bits (128 bytes), and multiplying by a large number of blocks quickly becomes impractical. That drives several compression strategies. Coarse bit vectors group cores so one bit represents multiple cores — this reduces storage but sometimes requires broadcasting within a group. Limited pointers store only a few sharer IDs; if the number of sharers exceeds the limit, the directory falls back to broadcasting or a different mechanism. Hierarchical directories break the system into levels so a top-level directory points to lower-level directories that manage subsets of cores. Each approach trades storage for additional messaging, potential broadcasts to groups, or added complexity. A misconception is assuming compression is free; compressed representations increase protocol complexity and can add latency or additional messages. When designing, always weigh the storage saved against the extra messaging cost and complexity introduced by the chosen compression technique.

The directory controller must process every coherence request for the addresses it owns. In a centralized design, that controller can become a bandwidth and latency bottleneck as core counts increase. Directory bandwidth describes how many requests per second the directory controller can handle; when requests queue up, directory access latency increases. Two widely used solutions are distribution and caching. Distributed directories place directory responsibility across multiple memory controllers or cache banks, each covering a subset of addresses. This spreads load and reduces the chance of a single hotspot. Directory caching keeps frequently accessed directory entries close to requestors so lookups avoid the full directory controller on every request. Distributed directories reduce traffic concentration but complicate address mapping and failure modes. Directory caching reduces repeated lookup costs but introduces coherence for directory entries themselves. A common misconception is that distribution removes all bottlenecks — it reduces them but introduces design complexity such as remapping and cross-controller coordination. The practical lesson is to balance distribution granularity and directory caching based on expected access locality and workload hotspots. Directory bandwidth and distribution means distribute directory entries and cache hot entries to avoid single-controller bottlenecks; both approaches add design complexity and trade-offs.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Every directory-based coherence operation pays the cost of a directory lookup. For modest core counts, that extra lookup can make directory protocols slower than snooping. The chapter notes directory access time can be on the order of 10 to 20 cycles in systems with over 100 cores, which is acceptable for large systems but noticeable for latency-sensitive workloads. The end-to-end latency of a coherence request includes the cache request, directory lookup, any forwarding to owners or sharers, and the data return. Because directories often avoid broadcasts, they usually reduce total network bandwidth but add serialized steps: lookup, forwarding, and acknowledgements. Designers can mitigate this by distributing directories to reduce lookup contention and by caching directory entries to avoid repeated full lookups.
